variants.name: Jackson Serialization Views on the shared class
variants.implementation_notes: With Jackson, a field is a member of one or more named views and the caller chooses which view to serialize, so the same class carries several projections and no copying code exists; Spring MVC applies the same mechanism when a handler method (or its return value) is annotated with @JsonView. What replaces the classic filter object is the view class plus the writer configuration. By default un-annotated properties belong to every view, so MapperFeature.DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION must be disabled (or a view declared on the POJO) for the projection to be opt-in - otherwise each new field silently joins every receiver's payload. The classic key-by-key copy is still justified when the projection itself is data (a per-request field list), which views cannot express.
pitfalls: Leaving MapperFeature.DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION enabled inverts the contract: every field nobody annotated is included in every view, so the projection leaks by default instead of opting in.

Views live in the serialized class as annotations, so the domain model must import the JSON library and a new receiver means editing the producer's entity - views do not scale past a handful of named projections.
A view class is not a runtime filter: supplying a per-request field list requires Jackson's filter provider machinery instead, and mixing the two mechanisms produces payloads nobody can predict.

variants.name: narrow record DTO with an explicit mapper
variants.implementation_notes: Since records (JDK 16) a projection can be its own immutable carrier: declare the receiver's fields as a record component list and construct it from the domain object, so the wire contract exists as a type that is separate from the entity and can be versioned with the receiver. What replaces the classic filter object is the record plus its factory method; nothing about the domain model learns the receiver's name, and several receivers get several records. Choose it when the payload must not be shaped by Jackson annotations (the domain model stays free of serialization concerns) or when the projection must be unit-tested as a value; views remain the lighter option when one class must expose many closely related shapes.
pitfalls: A record duplicates the field list: when the producer adds or renames a field, the record keeps compiling and the receiver silently misses the data unless a contract test compares the record to the source schema.
Records are transparent carriers - their equals/hashCode/toString expose every component, so a record used inside logs or debug output leaks the fields the projection was meant to hide.
A nested record component still references the full child object: flattening a hierarchy requires the projection to copy the child's fields, otherwise the whole child graph ships with it.
